Bread rises because yeast eats the sugars in flour and releases carbon dioxide gas.
The gluten network that forms when wheat flour is mixed with water traps that gas in thousands of small bubbles.
Warm dough rises faster, because yeast works more quickly between about 25 and 30 degrees Celsius.
Kneading stretches the gluten strands so that they line up and hold more gas without tearing.
During baking the bubbles expand once more, the yeast dies, and the starch sets around the holes.
That is why a well kneaded and well proved loaf has an open, even crumb rather than a dense one.
Bakers judge proving by pressing the dough gently: if the dent springs back slowly, it is ready for the oven.

Brot geht auf, weil die Hefe den Zucker im Mehl frisst und dabei Kohlendioxid freisetzt.
Das Klebereiweiß im Weizenmehl bildet ein Netz, das dieses Gas in vielen kleinen Blasen festhält.
Warmer Teig geht schneller auf, weil die Hefe bei etwa 25 bis 30 Grad am besten arbeitet.
Beim Kneten werden die Kleberstränge gedehnt, sodass sie mehr Gas halten können, ohne zu reißen.
Im Ofen dehnen sich die Blasen noch einmal aus, die Hefe stirbt, und die Stärke wird fest.
Deshalb hat ein gut gekneteter Laib eine lockere, gleichmäßige Krume und keine dichte.

Tides are caused mainly by the gravity of the Moon pulling on the oceans of the Earth.
The water on the side facing the Moon is pulled a little more strongly than the Earth itself, so it bulges outward.
On the far side the Earth is pulled away from the water, which leaves a second bulge behind.
As the Earth turns, most coasts pass through both bulges, so they see two high tides a day.
The Sun adds its own smaller pull, and when Sun and Moon line up the tides are larger, which sailors call spring tides.
When they pull at right angles the range is smaller, and these are called neap tides.
Local coastlines and the depth of the sea can make the real pattern far more complicated than this simple picture.
